git-init.title: Choose an empty room
git-init.body: Point git at any folder — even one with nothing in it yet.

visual.caption: A bare folder, before git arrives

git-init.title: The .git folder appears
git-init.body: Git creates the entire repository in a hidden .git directory: objects/ (empty), refs/ (empty), HEAD, and the index.

visual.caption: Four core structures materialize

git-init.title: Nothing is tracked yet
git-init.body: No objects, no commits. Git is only ready, waiting for your first git add and git commit.

visual.caption: An empty museum, waiting for its first exhibit

git-status.title: Look
git-status.body: You want to know what changed. Just run git status — it compares three snapshots: your files, the index, and the last commit.

visual.caption: Git reports where every file stands

git-status.title: Read the columns
git-status.body: Each file gets a state marker. ✚ staged = ready to commit. ✏ modified = changed on disk. Blue = brand new, never tracked.

visual.caption: Green = in the index · Red = changed · Blue = untracked

git-status.title: The comparison trick
git-status.body: Status never reads whole files — it compares a fast hash from the index with a hash of the disk file. Identical hashes? Unchanged.

visual.caption: Status is a diff across three places

git-add.title: Change a file
git-add.body: You edit src/button.tsx. Git sees the worktree no longer matches the index — the file is 'modified' but not staged.

visual.caption: Your edit lives in the working tree only

git-add.title: Run git add
git-add.body: The file's content is hashed into a blob object, and the index stores path → blob-hash. Your file now belongs to the 'next commit' preview.

visual.caption: git add copies the snapshot into the index

git-add.title: Nothing moved on disk
git-add.body: The working file stays exactly as it was. Staging only writes the index — it's a note saying 'this content is the next snapshot'.

visual.caption: The file remains untouched — only the index changed

git-commit.title: Stage first
git-commit.body: Before a commit, files live in the index (staging). The index is a preview of what the commit will contain.

visual.caption: The index holds your next snapshot

git-commit.title: Run git commit
git-commit.body: Git wraps the index into a tree object, then builds a commit object that points to that tree and to the previous commit (its parent).

visual.caption: tree + parent + author + message, then hashed

git-commit.title: Watch the commit appear
git-commit.body: A new commit object joins the graph. The branch pointer slides forward and HEAD follows it. History is one node longer.

spec.caption: The branch and HEAD move forward onto the new commit

git-config.title: Set your name
git-config.body: Before your first commit, Git needs an identity — the name and email written into every commit you make.

visual.caption: Identity lives in git config, applied from the narrowest scope

git-config.title: Set your email
git-config.body: Commits are stamped with this identity as author and committer lines — baked into the commit object forever.

visual.caption: user.email joins user.name; both are baked into commits

git-config.title: See every alias
git-config.body: Config is a cascade: this repo → your user (~/.gitconfig) → the machine. The nearest one wins.

visual.caption: Scopes cascade: system → global → local

git-branch.title: Pick your starting point
git-branch.body: A branch is just a pointer to a commit. From wherever HEAD is, you can hang a new name.

git-branch.title: Run git branch
git-branch.body: A tiny ref file is written with the current commit's hash. Now two names point at the same commit.

spec.caption: feature is a second pointer — one commit, two names

git-branch.title: You're still on main
git-branch.body: Branch only creates the pointer — it doesn't move you. That's git switch's job.

git-checkout.title: Where do you want to stand?
git-checkout.body: Checkout flips HEAD from one branch to another — and rewrites your working files to match that branch.

spec.caption: HEAD is about to glide to feature

git-checkout.title: HEAD moves, files follow
git-checkout.body: The HEAD file now says ref: refs/heads/feature. Blobs from feature's commit are copied onto disk so your worktree matches.

spec.caption: HEAD now rests on feature — the worktree rebuilt itself

git-checkout.title: Safety first
git-checkout.body: If a file has unsaved edits, checkout refuses instead of destroying them. -f means 'I really mean it'.

git-switch.title: A focused checkout
git-switch.body: SWITCH is checkout's branch-only half. One job: move HEAD between branches.

git-switch.title: The whole hop is one pointer edit
git-switch.body: HEAD.txt is rewritten to name the other branch. Files on disk are synchronized from that branch's blobs.

spec.caption: One file rewrite + a worktree sync — done

git-switch.title: Create and hop in one
git-switch.body: git switch -c name does branch + switch together — the modern replacement for checkout -b.

git-merge.title: Two branches, two timelines
git-merge.body: Your feature branch and main have both moved since they split from the same commit.

spec.caption: Diverged from commit 4b7c2a5 — the merge base

git-merge.title: Three-way merge: the userland is untouched
git-merge.body: Git compares the base commit against BOTH tips, then combines the two sets of changes. Different regions — or pure insertions on one side — merge themselves automatically. No human needed.

spec.caption: Different hunks stitch together into a two-parent merge commit

git-merge.title: Conflict: the merge stops and hands you the file
git-merge.body: But both sides edited the SAME lines — and Git refuses to guess who wins. It writes BOTH versions into the file, separated by <<<<<<< HEAD, ======= and >>>>>>> markers, marks the path unmerged, and halts the merge. Nothing is written to history yet — you still have a clean escape: git merge --abort.

visual.caption: The same hunk, both answers, three markers — Git hands you the decision

git-merge.title: git status reads the battlefield
git-merge.body: The merge is stuck, and git status tells you exactly where. Under 'Unmerged paths' it says 'both modified' — both branches changed this file into the working tree. You cannot commit while a path is unmerged; resolve first, then it goes green.

visual.caption: Unmerged paths: both modified — the merge is paused, not broken

git-merge.title: Decide, then git add marks it resolved
git-merge.body: Open the file, read both sides, and keep what's right — one side, the other, or a blend. Delete the marker lines, save, then git add the file to tell Git 'I decided'. A resolved file is just a normal staged file; the conflict is what you remove.

visual.caption: Markers gone, one truth chosen — add stages exactly what the merge should record

git-merge.title: Finish: merge --continue writes the merge commit
git-merge.body: git merge --continue picks up where the merge paused: it opens the commit editor pre-filled with 'Merge branch Feature', you save it, and a real two-parent merge commit lands — just like any uncontested merge. Resolution is just a normal commit; the branch story stays fork-shaped forever.

spec.caption: A resolved conflict is still just a merge commit — two parents, one decision

git-rebase.title: Newer base, same ideas
git-rebase.body: You want your feature to sit on top of the newest main — not on a stale fork point.

spec.caption: feature grew from the old main

git-rebase.title: Replay, don't copy
git-rebase.body: Each feature commit is re-created on top of main's new tip. Same diff, new parent, new hash. Same changes, cleaner story.

spec.caption: feature now sits on the newest main — linear history

git-rebase.title: Handle conflicts one commit at a time
git-rebase.body: If a replayed commit collides, the rebase pauses so you fix it, then continue. Commit by commit.

visual.caption: Paused mid-replay: resolve, then git rebase --continue

git-rebase.title: Rewrite rule
git-rebase.body: Rebased commits get new hashes. Never rebase what others have pulled — that's how force-pushes are born.

git-log.title: Ask who did what
git-log.body: git log starts at HEAD and follows every parent pointer, printing each commit.

spec.caption: The newest commit is on top

git-log.title: It's a linked list
git-log.body: The trick: commits only know their parents. Log is just walking that chain — down, down, down to the first commit.

spec.caption: Follow the parent pointers to rewind time

git-show.title: Open one commit
git-show.body: git show displays the full anatomy of a single object — for a commit, that's metadata plus its diff.

visual.caption: tree, parent, author, committer, message — then the diff

git-show.title: Pull a file from the past
git-show.body: The rev:path syntax prints any file exactly as it existed: git show HEAD~2:src/App.tsx.

visual.caption: Any object can be shown: commits, tags, trees, blobs

git-diff.title: What did I touch?
git-diff.body: git diff compares your working files against the index — every edit you haven't staged yet.

visual.caption: Worktree vs index = the red and green you just made

git-diff.title: See what's staged
git-diff.body: git diff --cached compares the index against HEAD — a preview of your next commit.

visual.caption: Index vs HEAD = exactly what the commit will change

git-diff.title: Blob hashing shortcuts the work
git-diff.body: Identical content means identical SHA-1 — matching blobs are skipped instantly. Only changed files enter the diff engine.

visual.caption: Same content → same hash → skipped

git-blame.title: Find the culprit (politely)
git-blame.body: git blame walks the file's history backwards and marks every line with the commit that introduced it.

visual.caption: Every line now wears its origin commit

git-blame.title: Follow the trail
git-blame.body: Jump from the blamed commit to its message with git show — the 'why' is usually written right there.

visual.caption: blame → show → the story

git-reflog.title: The undo stack
git-reflog.body: Every time HEAD moves — commit, reset, rebase, checkout, amend — git journals it. git reflog prints that journal.

visual.caption: HEAD@{n} = where you were n moves ago

git-reflog.title: Recover anything
git-reflog.body: Hard-reset too far? Find the old position in the reflog and point HEAD back at it. The commit is still in objects/.

visual.caption: A hard reset only forgets the pointer — the reflog remembers

git-reflog.title: The 90-day window
git-reflog.body: Unreachable commits aren't deleted — they just wait. git gc finally prunes them after the default 90 days.

visual.caption: Until gc, 'lost' commits are recoverable

git-gc.title: The repository gets fat
git-gc.body: Every add and commit writes loose, individually-compressed files. Thousands later, .git bloats and slows.

visual.caption: Loose objects pile up as you work

git-gc.title: Compress and prune
git-gc.body: git gc packs loose objects into one delta-compressed packfile and deletes unreachable, aged-out objects.

visual.caption: Packed: only the differences between versions are stored

git-reset.title: Too far, too fast
git-reset.body: A bad commit sits at the tip of your branch. You want the branch pointer to slide back over it.

spec.caption: The oops commit is on top

git-reset.title: The pointer rewinds
git-reset.body: The branch file is rewritten to point at the older commit. The oops commit is still in objects/ — just unreachable.

spec.caption: main + HEAD slide back; the oops commit dangles

git-reset.title: Three depths of regret
git-reset.body: soft keeps things staged, mixed (default) unstages, hard also reverts your files.

visual.caption: --soft / --mixed / --hard = which stores to roll back

git-restore.title: Messed up a file
git-restore.body: Your working copy of src/bug.js is broken. Restore rewrites it from the index (or HEAD).

visual.caption: The index copy is healthy — let's take it back

git-restore.title: Unstage by accident?
git-restore.body: restore --staged pulls HEAD's version back into the index, unstaging the file without touching disk.

visual.caption: --staged = undo the staging

git-restore.title: Resurrect from history
git-restore.body: --source lets you pull any revision's blob. Gone file, old version, whatever — read it back out.

visual.caption: --source=<rev> = restore from any commit

git-revert.title: Shared branch, broken commit
git-revert.body: A bad commit already went to every teammate. Rewriting it with reset would break their clones — so we add instead.

spec.caption: The target: a bad commit buried in history

git-revert.title: A correction, not an erasure
git-revert.body: git revert applies the reverse diff as a brand-new commit on top. The bad commit stays in history — truthfully.

spec.caption: The inverse commit neutralizes the damage

git-stash.title: Interrupted mid-feature
git-stash.body: Half-finished changes sit in your worktree, but you must switch branches now.

visual.caption: Uncommitted work you don't want to lose

git-stash.title: Parked in a box
git-stash.body: Your changes are recorded as special commits on the stash stack, and the worktree is reset to a clean HEAD.

visual.caption: stash@{0} holds the WIP — the worktree is clean

git-stash.title: Come back to it later
git-stash.body: Any branch, any time: git stash pop reapplies the top of the stack and removes it.

visual.caption: pop = apply + drop · apply = keep it on the stack

git-cherry-pick.title: One fix, other branch too
git-cherry-pick.body: A hotfix landed on main, but the release branch needs it right now — without merging all of main.

spec.caption: The fix commit — about to travel

git-cherry-pick.title: Replayed on release
git-cherry-pick.body: A new commit lands on release with the identical change but a brand-new hash and parent.

spec.caption: The fix now exists on both branches

git-clean.title: Stray files everywhere
git-clean.body: Untracked files and build junk litter your worktree. First, preview what clean would remove.

visual.caption: ??? = untracked · clean only touches these

git-clean.title: The full sweep
git-clean.body: clean -fd deletes untracked files AND directories; -x also removes ignored ones. Permanent, so preview first.

visual.caption: clean -fd: files + dirs · clean -fdx: plus ignored

git-clone.title: Grab the whole project
git-clone.body: You point at a remote URL. Everything — every commit, branch, tag — is about to flow down to you.

visual.caption: The object database streams down

git-clone.title: Fetch + checkout in one
git-clone.body: Clone is literally a fetch (download all objects) followed by a checkout (materialize the default branch).

visual.caption: Objects land, then the working tree is built

git-clone.title: Origin is wired for you
git-clone.body: refs/remotes/origin/main is created and your main learns to track it — that's what makes git pull work on day one.

visual.caption: origin remote is bookmarked in your config

git-remote.title: Bookmark another repo
git-remote.body: A remote is just a name → URL note. No network happens until you fetch or push.

visual.caption: git remote add links a name to a URL

git-remote.title: The fork workflow
git-remote.body: origin is yours, upstream is the original. Keep both bookmarks and you can sync from anywhere.

visual.caption: Two bookmarks, one project

git-fetch.title: See without changing
git-fetch.body: You want to peek at the remote's new commits without disturbing anything you're doing.

visual.caption: Objects download; your branch and files stay put

git-fetch.title: Remote refs update, you don't
git-fetch.body: refs/remotes/origin/main slides forward. Your own main, index and worktree are untouched.

visual.caption: Only the remote-tracking ref moved

git-fetch.title: Preview the future
git-fetch.body: git diff HEAD..origin/main shows what a pull would bring — before you commit to it.

visual.caption: HEAD..origin/main = 'what's coming'

git-pull.title: Sync with the team
git-pull.body: git pull fetches the remote's new work, then merges it into your current branch.

visual.caption: Objects come down…

git-pull.title: …then a merge folds it in
git-pull.body: If you made no local commits, main just fast-forwards. If you did, a merge commit (or a rebase) joins them.

spec.caption: Both histories now belong to your branch

git-pull.title: Rebase instead of merge
git-pull.body: git pull --rebase replays your local edits on top instead of merging — a clean, straight line.

git-push.title: Share your commits
git-push.body: You've committed locally. The remote doesn't have those objects yet — they're about to travel up.

visual.caption: Your branch is ahead — the upload starts

git-push.title: Upload + advance
git-push.body: Your new objects stream to the remote, and origin/main advances to match your branch.

visual.caption: Remote branch ref slides to your tip

git-push.title: Rejected? You're behind
git-push.body: The remote refuses to lose history. Pull --rebase first, then push — the daily rhythm of shared branches.

visual.caption: 'non-fast-forward' = the remote moved first

git-push.title: Force-pushing, safely
git-push.body: Need to rewrite a remote branch? Only --force-with-lease: it forces only if the remote matches what you last saw.

visual.caption: --force-with-lease: forced, but never blind

git-tag.title: Freeze a milestone
git-tag.body: You shipped v1.0.0. A branch would drift — you need a name that never moves.

spec.caption: Time to pin this moment

git-tag.title: The pin drops
git-tag.body: A tag ref points at that commit forever — even when main races ahead, v1.0.0 still points here.

spec.caption: A permanent landmark on the commit
